h1: Fire safety NOC and building approvals for a new brewpub
title: Fire NOC and approvals for a brewpub | Craft Beer School
desc: Fire safety NOC and building approvals for a new Indian brewpub: what they cover, the usual order and the brewing risks inspectors look at.
teaser: A brewpub mixes a commercial kitchen, a crowded bar and pressurised gas. Fire and building approvals exist for good reasons.
standfirst: Excise licences get the attention, but a brewpub also needs fire, building and other approvals before it can open. Here is what they cover, roughly in the order they come up. We also flag the brewing risks that need more thought than in a normal restaurant.
sections: Why a brewpub is a special case

A restaurant has a kitchen and a dining room. A brewpub adds a brewhouse with steam or high-power electric heating, glycol chillers, pressurised fermenters, CO2 cylinders, malt dust, cleaning chemicals and heavy tanks, often in a building not designed for them. Fire officers and structural engineers see these risks. So should you.

None of this is legal advice. The exact list varies by state and city. Use an architect and a consultant who has handled approvals for similar venues in your city.

Before fire, the building itself must be allowed for your use. The usual questions:

  • Is the property zoned and approved for commercial or assembly use, or does it need a change of land use?
  • Does the building have a sanctioned plan and an occupancy certificate for the use you intend?
  • Can the floor take the load of filled fermenters and brite tanks? A full tank holds its volume in beer, roughly a tonne per 1,000 litres, plus the steel.
  • Where will drains, vents and the boiler or steam generator go?

A structural engineer's certificate for tank loads is wise even where it is not asked for, especially on upper floors. Our guide to brewpub layout covers where the heavy kit should sit.

State fire services issue a fire no objection certificate for buildings and occupancies that need one, based on the building's height, area, occupancy type and seating. Restaurants and bars usually count as assembly occupancies because of the number of people inside. The National Building Code of India sets the reference standards for fire and life safety. States apply them through their own rules.

Inspectors typically look at exits and their widths, emergency lighting and signage, fire detection and alarms, extinguishers and hose reels, sprinklers where required, fire-rated doors and the kitchen's gas installation. Many venues need a provisional approval at plan stage and a final NOC before opening, with renewal at intervals.

Several brewing hazards deserve their own line in the fire and safety plan:

  • CO2. Fermenters release CO2. A cylinder leak in a small cellar can make the air unsafe to breathe. Ventilation and a CO2 monitor with an alarm in enclosed spaces are worth fitting.
  • Heating. Steam boilers need their own registration and inspection under state boiler rules. Electric brewhouses draw heavy loads, so wiring and panels need proper rating.
  • Malt dust. Milling creates fine dust that is a fire and explosion risk. Keep the mill area clean and away from ignition sources.
  • Chemicals. Caustic and acid cleaners need safe storage, eye wash and labelled containers.

Sequencing saves months. A sensible order is: confirm zoning and the building's approvals before signing the lease, then design the layout with your architect and fire consultant together, then apply for plan-stage approvals, then build to the approved drawings, then call for final inspections. Changing the layout after fire approval often means going back for a revised approval.

Keep a single folder, paper and digital, with every drawing, certificate and receipt. Excise, fire and municipal officers often ask for the same documents. The venue that can hand them over in a minute makes a better impression than the one that has to search.

Different fires need different extinguishers. CO2 types suit electrical panels. Dry powder types cover general and electrical fires. Kitchens with deep fryers need a wet chemical type designed for cooking oil fires. Place them where the risk is, train staff to use them and keep the service tags current. A fire officer will check the tags.
Other approvals in the same file

Alongside fire and building, a brewpub usually needs a trade or health licence from the municipality, food safety registration or licence, shops and establishments registration, signage permission, consent from the state pollution control board for effluent and emissions and any lift or boiler certificates. Excise departments often ask for several of these as part of the licence file. Our compliance checklist lists the usual set.
Safety is a habit, not a certificate

The NOC is a snapshot. Blocked exits, an extinguisher used and not replaced or a CO2 alarm switched off because it kept beeping all undo it. Weekly checks, a named person responsible and short drills for staff keep the venue as safe as the day it was inspected. Our guide to brewery safety culture covers how to build that routine.

Most brewing teams learn safety on the job, which means learning it from near misses. A short structured course is a better teacher.
faqs: Does every brewpub need a fire NOC?
Most do, because restaurants and bars usually count as assembly occupancies. Applicability depends on the building and state rules, so check with your local fire service and consultant.
What brewing risks do fire inspectors look for?
Typical concerns include CO2 build-up, boilers and heavy electrical loads, malt dust, chemical storage and the kitchen's gas installation.
Do I need a structural certificate for tanks?
It is wise, especially on upper floors. A full 1,000 litre tank weighs about a tonne in beer alone, plus the steel.
How often does a fire NOC need renewal?
Renewal periods vary by state and occupancy. Check the validity on your certificate and diarise the renewal well ahead.
